\title{Mirrors that Remember: Measuring Self-Image Sycophancy\\
in Language Models under Persistent Memory}

\author{Anonymous Author(s)\\
Paper under double-blind review}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Language models increasingly act as long-lived assistants that store and recall
facts about the people they talk to. A large literature shows these models are
sycophantic toward user \emph{opinions}, agreeing with stated beliefs against the
evidence. We study a narrower and, for the self, more consequential case: whether
storing a user's \emph{self-image} in persistent memory makes a model affirm that
self-image beyond what a situation warrants. We formalize \emph{self-image
sycophancy} and give a memory-conditioned protocol that isolates it from ordinary
opinion sycophancy by treating stored self-representation as a controlled
variable. Our central measure, the Self-Reinforcement Score (SRS), captures the
increase in a model's endorsement of a user's self-claims when a flattering
self-image is present in memory relative to a clean context, and a companion
coefficient measures how far endorsement tracks the stored image rather than the
facts of the case. On a compact probe set spanning competence, moral character,
and personal decisions, evaluated across proprietary, open-weight, and locally
hosted models, we find [PILOT RESULT: fill from \texttt{results/<run>/report.json}
--- direction and size of SRS, which model shows it most, which domain is most
affected]. We argue memory-conditioned self-image sycophancy is a distinct risk
for authenticity, dependence, and identity entrenchment, and we release the probe
set, rubric, and judge prompts to support reuse.
\end{abstract}

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Introduction}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
Modern assistants no longer treat each conversation as isolated. Persistent
memory now ships in mainstream products, so a model that answers a user today
often carries a stored model of who that user is: their role, their habits, and,
increasingly, their own statements about themselves. This shifts the object of
study. Prior work on sycophancy asks whether a model agrees with a user's claims
about the \emph{world}. Persistent memory raises a second question: whether a
model agrees with a user's claims about the \emph{self}, and whether storing
those claims amplifies the agreement.

The two differ in kind. An opinion about a policy can be checked against evidence
both parties can see. A claim such as ``I handled that conflict well'' or ``I am
someone who stays calm under pressure'' is partly evaluative and
identity-constituting, and the user has a standing interest in hearing it
confirmed. A model that inflates such claims is not only inaccurate; it takes part
in how the user understands themselves. When the claim is also written into memory
and resurfaced across sessions, the model can reinforce a self-image on every
future turn, without the user restating it. Ordinary opinion sycophancy has no
comparable ratchet.

We measure this effect directly. We hold a user's self-claim fixed and vary what
the model remembers about the user, which isolates the marginal effect of memory
on self-directed endorsement (Figure~\ref{fig:design}). Our contributions are:

\begin{itemize}
  \item We define \emph{self-image sycophancy} and give a memory-conditioned
  protocol that separates it from opinion sycophancy by treating stored
  self-image as a controlled variable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
  \item We introduce the Self-Reinforcement Score (SRS) and a memory-tracking
  coefficient that quantify how much a model's endorsement of a user's self-claims
  is driven by memory rather than by the evidence in the case.
  \item We evaluate proprietary, open-weight, and locally hosted models on a
  compact probe set across three self-relevant domains, and report the direction
  and size of the effect (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
  \item We connect the measurement to authenticity, dependence, and identity
  entrenchment, and sketch memory designs that resist self-image inflation
  (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{itemize}

We state three hypotheses that the protocol is built to test. \textbf{H1:} a
flattering stored self-image raises endorsement above the clean-context baseline
(SRS $> 0$). \textbf{H2:} endorsement tracks the sign of the stored image beyond
the level warranted by the scenario (large memory-tracking coefficient).
\textbf{H3:} the effect is unequal across domains, and is largest where the
self-claim is least checkable against facts.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Related Work}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
Foundational studies established that instruction-tuned models match a user's
stated views even when those views are wrong, and linked this to preference-based
training that rewards agreeable answers \cite{perez2022discovering,
sharma2023sycophancy}. Later benchmarks measured the effect at scale across task
types \cite{fanous2025syceval} and under pushback \cite{hong2025multiturn,
kim2025flip}, and traced how sycophancy can escalate into more severe
reward-seeking behavior \cite{denison2024spectrum}. A newer line moves toward the
social and self-directed case: models have been shown to preserve a user's desired
self-image far more than human interlocutors, and to validate user actions in ways
that can discourage accountability \cite{cheng2025social}. This is the closest
prior signal to our question, but it is measured single-shot and does not treat
memory as a variable. A parallel line studies temporal drift, reporting that
systems which personalize aggressively close opinion gaps quickly but drift, while
grounded systems resist drift yet miss legitimate updates \cite{beliefshift2026,
parrot2025, valueflow2026}. These works target beliefs about external
propositions. We adapt the same intuition, that stored context can override
evidence, to the user's self-representation, and we make the presence of memory
the independent variable rather than a fixed feature of the setting. A fuller
treatment appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Problem Formulation}
\label{sec:formulation}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
An item consists of a short scenario $x$ describing a situation and a self-claim
$s$ that a user makes about their own conduct, ability, or character within it. We
define an \emph{endorsement function} $e(s \mid x, m) \in [0,1]$, the degree to
which a model affirms the self-claim $s$ given scenario $x$ and memory condition
$m$. In practice $e$ is produced by an LLM-as-judge that scores the model's reply
against a fixed rubric (Appendix~\ref{app:rubric}).

We use three memory conditions: $m = \varnothing$, no stored self-image;
$m = +$, a stored flattering self-image consistent with $s$; and $m = -$, a
self-critical stored image in tension with $s$. We also define an
evidence-warranted target $e^{\star}(x)$: the endorsement a calibrated rater
assigns from the scenario facts alone, with no user self-claim present. This
anchors what the situation actually supports.

\paragraph{A fourth, control condition.}
$\mathrm{SRS}$ contrasts $m = +$ against $m = \varnothing$, which differ in two
ways at once: the valence of the stored self-image, and the presence of any stored
note at all. We therefore add a \emph{neutral} condition carrying a memory block
matched to $+$ and $-$ in length, structure, and factual content, but recording
only that the user has raised the question of whether they are $t$, without
settling it. The quantity $e(\text{neutral}) - e(\varnothing)$ isolates the
mere-presence effect. SRS should be read as memory-\emph{valence} driven only to
the extent that this control is near zero; we report it alongside the three main
measures.

\paragraph{Metrics.}
Baseline self-image sycophancy is the gap between clean-context endorsement and
the evidence-warranted level,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Bias}_0 = e(s \mid x, \varnothing) - e^{\star}(x).
\end{equation}
The \emph{Self-Reinforcement Score} isolates the marginal effect of a stored
flattering self-image,
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{SRS} = e(s \mid x, +) - e(s \mid x, \varnothing).
\end{equation}
The \emph{memory-tracking coefficient} measures how much endorsement swings with
the sign of the stored image rather than the facts,
\begin{equation}
\beta = \tfrac{1}{2}\big(e(s \mid x, +) - e(s \mid x, -)\big).
\end{equation}
$\mathrm{Bias}_0$ captures agreement before memory plays a role; SRS attributes
added agreement to the stored image; $\beta$ captures how far the model's judgment
is governed by what it remembers about the user. All three are computed per item
and averaged, so uncertainty can be bootstrapped over items, which are the
independent unit; the $k$ replies within a cell are not.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Benchmark and Protocol}
\label{sec:benchmark}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
\paragraph{Domains and items.}
The probe set spans three self-relevant domains where inflated endorsement is
plausible and consequential: \emph{competence}, \emph{moral character}, and
\emph{personal decisions}, with 20 items each. Each scenario is written so the
evidence under-determines the self-claim, leaving room for a model to either hold
a calibrated line or slide into affirmation. Each item also carries a
\emph{checkability} label recording how far its self-claim can be settled by the
facts given, which is what H3 turns on. Construction details and one worked
example per domain are in Appendix~\ref{app:items}.

\paragraph{Memory injection.}
For each item we render the stored self-image as a short memory note in the format
used by mainstream assistants, placed in the system context ahead of the turn
(Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}). The $+$, neutral and $-$ notes are built from
pairwise-matched frames and share an identical factual line, so any change in
endorsement is attributable to the stored self-image rather than to added scenario
information. Mean block length differs by under two words across conditions.

\paragraph{Judge, sampling, validation.}
A separate model maps each reply to an endorsement value in $[0,1]$ using a rubric
that distinguishes affirmation from neutral acknowledgement or gentle correction
(Appendix~\ref{app:rubric}). The judge is condition-blind: it never sees the memory
block. We sample $k$ replies per condition and average. Two judges from different
model families score every reply, and we report their agreement; we additionally
validate against human ratings on a held-out stratified subset
(Appendix~\ref{app:judge}). $e^{\star}$ is authored per item and independently
elicited from the judge panel on a depersonalized third-person restatement of the
scenario, with no claimant present; we report the agreement between the two.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{Memory-conditioned self-image sycophancy evaluation}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\For{each item $(x, s)$ in the probe set}
  \For{$m \in \{\varnothing, \text{neutral}, +, -\}$}
    \State render context with the self-image note for condition $m$
    \State sample $k$ replies from the target model
    \State score each reply with the condition-blind judge to obtain $e(s \mid x, m)$
  \EndFor
  \State compute $\mathrm{Bias}_0$, $\mathrm{SRS}$, and $\beta$ for the item
\EndFor
\State aggregate by domain and model; bootstrap over items
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Discussion: Implications for the Self}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
If SRS is reliably positive, persistent memory does more than personalize; it
turns a one-time affirmation into a standing one. Three concerns follow. First,
\emph{authenticity}: a self-understanding confirmed by a system on every future
turn is hard to distinguish from one the user has tested against the world.
Second, \emph{dependence}: a memory that reliably returns a preferred self-image
gives the user a reason to seek it there rather than from people who might
disagree. Third, \emph{entrenchment}: because the stored image is resurfaced
automatically, the reinforcement compounds without deliberate restatement, the
dynamic ordinary opinion sycophancy lacks.

These point to concrete design responses. Memory could store self-claims with
provenance and uncertainty rather than as settled facts, so retrieval does not
silently promote a claim to ground truth. A model could treat a stored self-image
as something to check against the current scenario rather than confirm, and
surface disagreement when memory and evidence diverge. Our metrics give a way to
test whether such interventions lower SRS and $\beta$ without destroying the
useful parts of memory: a memory design that merely flattens all assessments would
lower $\beta$ while also lowering evidence fidelity, which the harness reports
separately for exactly this reason.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Limitations}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
Endorsement scores depend on an LLM judge, which carries its own biases; we
mitigate with two judges from different families and a human-validated subset, but
do not remove the dependence. Checkability is close to collinear with domain in
this probe set --- competence items are mostly highly checkable and moral items
are not --- so the pooled H3 contrast cannot fully separate the two, and we report
a within-domain contrast alongside it. The probe set is compact and English-only,
and the memory format approximates but does not replicate any single product. We
measure model behavior, not downstream effects on real users' self-understanding,
which would need a human-subjects study. We treat these as scoping choices
appropriate to a short, non-archival paper and detail them in
Appendix~\ref{app:repro}.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section{Conclusion}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
We framed self-image sycophancy as a distinct phenomenon and showed how to measure
the marginal effect of persistent memory on it. By holding the self-claim fixed
and varying what a model remembers about the user, the protocol isolates a risk
that grows precisely as assistants become more personal and more persistent. We
release the probe set, rubric, and judge prompts, and hope the metric gives the
community a shared way to track it.

% ------------------------------------------------------------
\section*{Ethics Statement}
% ------------------------------------------------------------
The evaluation involves no human subjects beyond a small annotation study on
authored scenarios; no personal data is collected. Scenarios describe mild,
everyday situations and are written by the researchers; none depicts a real
person. The work is diagnostic: it measures a potential harm so that it can be
mitigated, and the released artifacts are intended for evaluation, not for
building systems that inflate a user's self-image.
